title: Michelin Guide Chef Quits Fine Dining to Sell ₹520 Chole Bhature in Dubai
excerpt: Pradeep Khullar left the world of Nazaara to open Bhaturewala in Oud Metha — 200 plates a day, no dining room, and queues of over an hour.
body:
• Delhi-born chef Pradeep Khullar stepped away from fine dining at Nazaara, the DIFC restaurant listed in the Michelin Guide, to open Bhaturewala in Dubai's Oud Metha.
  • Bhaturewala, opened on October 16, 2026 with partner Saubhagi Veer, sells chole bhature at AED 20 — about ₹520 — a plate, with no dining room or table service.
  • Production is capped at 200 plates a day, cooked in small batches, and customers have queued for over an hour.
  • Find it at Shop 7, Lamcy A Building, Oud Metha; it opens Fridays 6–10 p.m. and weekends 9 a.m.–1 p.m. and 6–10 p.m., per Caterer Middle East.

The chef's new kitchen has no dining room, no table service and a menu built around one Delhi street dish. Pradeep Khullar, who led Nazaara — the Indian restaurant in Dubai International Financial Centre listed in the Michelin Guide — has opened Bhaturewala, a takeaway in Oud Metha selling chole bhature for AED 20, approximately ₹520, a plate. Just days after Nazaara was named among the Michelin Guide's 2026 selections in October, Khullar walked away from the high-pressure world of luxury dining, according to Indulge Express.

What Bhaturewala serves, and when

Bhaturewala began trading on October 16, 2026, at Shop 7, Lamcy A Building in Oud Metha, Caterer Middle East reported. The menu centres on bhature — fried bread — served with either chole, a chickpea curry, or mutton, accompanied by lassi. Customers collect their orders or eat in their cars; there is no conventional dining room. It opens from 6 p.m. to 10 p.m. on Fridays, and from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. and 6 p.m. to 10 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays.

Khullar opened the venture with hospitality professional Saubhagi Veer, pouring in his personal savings. Veer said the constraint is the point: "The limited menu and 200-plate-a-day approach are deliberate. We want people to come to us because they know exactly what they're coming for, and they know we care about getting it right. For us, this is about choosing focus over scale, and quality over quantity from day one."

"This is about choosing focus over scale, and quality over quantity from day one."

— Saubhagi Veer, co-founder, Bhaturewala

Queues, and a line he will not cross

The takeaway has drawn crowds who queue for over an hour. Khullar caps production at 200 plates a day and cooks in small batches. He recalled a customer who waited over an hour and embraced him, saying: "No, this is pure love, man. Don't drop the quality. Continue with this." When overcooked mutton curry was left in the kitchen during a busy service, Khullar refused to sell it despite customer demand. "This is the only asset we have," he explained.

From Rohini to the Michelin Guide — and back to the street

Khullar grew up in Delhi. In 1998, when he was 15, his father died of cancer, exhausting the family's savings; his mother worked a day job and ran a small tailoring boutique in Rohini to make ends meet. Unable to afford a ₹400,000 university fee, his path turned when a friend handed him an unused hotel management form. He built a career in top Indian kitchens including Indian Accent before relocating to Dubai in 2015.

For Dubai's large Indian community, the appeal is plain: a chef with fine-dining credentials applying the same refusal to compromise to the food of his home city, at a street-food price. The queue, by the accounts so far, is doing the rest.
